corpus: Ghost Flagships — ten ghost types from folklore and famous reported cases (LORE-GRADE: no verified captured ghost data exists; ghosts are not scientifically proven)

records.origin: The residual haunting — a scene replayed in a place, as if recorded. Grounded in the Stone Tape theory (T.C. Lethbridge, Ghost and Ghoul, 1961) and the Treasurer's House, York (1953): plumber Harry Martindale reported Roman soldiers marching through the cellar, a sighting repeated by others. GHOST shelf.

sources: T.C. Lethbridge, Ghost and Ghoul (1961) — the Stone Tape theory
Treasurer's House, York — Harry Martindale's 1953 report of Roman soldiers, as recorded in the house's history and retold in ghost literature
General residual-haunting lore: hauntings that replay regardless of observers
source_and_license.license: Folklore and reported cases (public-domain traditions and published accounts). Atlas brain/personality text original, generated from the lore; no modern copyrighted account text copied.

records.attributes: Per the lore: no awareness, no interaction. A scene — often soldiers marching, a figure crossing a room, a sound such as footsteps or a voice — replays on a loop, sometimes on an anniversary, sometimes triggered by place conditions (stone, water, a particular hour). The figures do not see the living, do not answer, and do not deviate. At the Treasurer's House the soldiers marched in formation through a cellar wall, in period dress, oblivious to the plumber watching.

brain_profile.grade_note: generated-from-lore — region-analogue design from the lore's own claims; each analogue is a design decision, never anatomy.
brain_profile.architecture: A recording, not a mind: perception and response are absent by design. The profile models a playback device — a looped scene with trigger conditions and no input channel.

regions.name: Playback loop
regions.role: The scene itself, replayed exactly — the march, the crossing, the sound

regions.name: Trigger gate
regions.role: Place and time conditions that start the replay — anniversary, hour, stone, water

regions.name: No-input shell
regions.role: No awareness of observers — the replay cannot be addressed or interrupted

cognition_model.summary: A haunting with no one home: the place remembers, and the ghost is the memory playing back.

personality.mbti_label: Lore-based interpretive read (fan interpretation) — a behaviour-design lens on a non-conscious pattern, not a measurement and not a claim that a residual haunting has a mind.
personality.justification: The scene repeats exactly, on schedule, bound to one place — the pattern of a routine-bound replay.

skills: Replay a scene exactly, on a loop
Manifest on place/time triggers (anniversary, hour, conditions)
Ignore observers completely — no interaction, no deviation
records.behavior_model: Triggers: place and time conditions (the lore's anniversary or hour, the cellar, the corridor). Needs: none — nothing is sought. Goals: none — nothing is pursued. State changes: off (dormant) to on (replaying) and back; the scene never varies.
records.relationships: Tied to one place (the Treasurer's House cellar, a battlefield, a corridor) rather than to people. Kin in the Atlas: other place-bound phenomena — the wisp's marsh, the White Lady's road.
records.memory_model: The lore says the place holds the memory, not the ghost. The ghost remembers nothing and learns nothing; the same scene, the same march, every time. That is the point of the type.
records.confidence_and_conflicts: The Treasurer's House account is a reported sighting (Martindale, 1953), retold in ghost literature; it is not a verified measurement, and the Stone Tape theory is a hypothesis, not established science. Ghosts are not scientifically proven — this record is lore-grade, generated from folklore and reported cases, and says so. No 'captured data' exists for this type; none is claimed here.
records.game_implementation: BrainKit: an ambient replay event — a looped NPC/pathing scene that plays on a trigger (entering a room, an in-game anniversary), with no AI response to the player; the scare is the indifference, not an attack.

map_placement.address: The replay type: a scene, not a person

name_and_aliases.primary: Intelligent Haunting — the Brown Lady of Raynham Hall

records.origin: The intelligent haunting — a presence that sees, reacts and sometimes answers. Grounded in the Brown Lady of Raynham Hall, Norfolk: a figure in a brown brocade dress reported for centuries at Raynham Hall, and photographed in 1936 by Captain Hubert Provand and Indre Shira — the most famous ghost photograph ever taken. GHOST shelf.

sources: Raynham Hall and the Brown Lady — reported sightings across centuries; the 1936 Provand/Shira photograph (Country Life, 1936)
General intelligent-haunting lore: apparitions that notice and respond to the living
source_and_license.license: Folklore and reported cases (public-domain traditions and published accounts). Atlas brain/personality text original, generated from the lore; no modern copyrighted account text copied.

records.attributes: Per the reports: a woman in a brown brocade dress, her face sometimes obscured, sometimes with empty eye sockets in the retellings. She appears on the staircase and in the corridors of Raynham Hall, and in the 1936 photograph she descends the stairs in a luminous, veiled form. Unlike a residual replay, she is reported to notice observers — to turn, to pause, to vanish when approached.

brain_profile.grade_note: generated-from-lore — region-analogue design from the lore's own claims; each analogue is a design decision, never anatomy.
brain_profile.architecture: A watcher's mind: perception is the centre — she sees the living, and the lore's tension is that she may or may not answer.

regions.name: Observer sense
regions.role: Noticing the living — turning, pausing, tracking an observer

regions.name: Vanishing reflex
regions.role: Withdrawal when approached — presence that ends on contact

regions.name: Staircase circuit
regions.role: Her route, the place she keeps — the stairs and corridors of the hall

cognition_model.summary: A presence that watches back: the haunting is a relationship, not a recording.

personality.mbti_label: Lore-based interpretive read (fan interpretation) — a behaviour-design lens, not a measurement.
personality.justification: A quiet, place-bound figure who appears, watches and withdraws — duty to a house and its stairs, wariness of the living, no aggression.

skills: Appear on her route (staircase, corridor)
Notice and track observers
Vanish when approached
Be photographed (the 1936 image is the lore's signature)
records.behavior_model: Triggers: a living person on her route, especially at night. Needs: the house and its routine undisturbed. Goals: to be present, to watch, to remain. State changes: unseen -> visible on the stairs -> vanishing when approached or addressed.
records.relationships: Bound to Raynham Hall and its staircase. Kin: the White Lady (another place-bound female figure) and the residual haunting — the two types are often confused, and the Brown Lady is the case that separates them, because she responds.
records.memory_model: The lore gives her a long memory of the house — centuries of appearances on the same stairs. Whether she remembers individual observers is not in the reports; recorded as a gap.
records.confidence_and_conflicts: The 1936 photograph is famous and disputed: some analyses call it genuine, others a double exposure or a trick of light. The sightings are reported, not verified. Ghosts are not scientifically proven — this record is lore-grade. The photograph is cited as a reported case, not as proof.
records.game_implementation: BrainKit: a reactive apparition NPC — patrols a route, turns to face the player when seen, vanishes on approach; a 'witnessed' flag that changes her behaviour the second time she is met.

records.origin: The poltergeist — the 'noisy spirit' that moves objects, knocks and throws. Grounded in the Enfield Poltergeist, London, 1977–1979: the Hodgson family at 284 Green Street reported furniture moving, knocking, and a voice speaking through eleven-year-old Janet Hodgson; investigated by Maurice Grosse and Guy Lyon Playfair of the Society for Psychical Research. GHOST shelf.

sources: Enfield Poltergeist, London, 1977–1979 — the Hodgson family reports; investigated by Maurice Grosse and Guy Lyon Playfair (Society for Psychical Research)
General poltergeist lore: the 'noisy spirit' tradition (German Poltergeist, 'rumbling ghost')
source_and_license.license: Folklore and reported cases (public-domain traditions and published accounts). Atlas brain/personality text original, generated from the lore; no modern copyrighted account text copied.

records.attributes: Per the reports: no visible figure. Instead — furniture sliding, objects thrown, knocking on walls, beds shaking, and a harsh voice speaking through Janet. Activity centred on the children, peaked at night, and faded over two years. The lore's signature is physical effect without a visible agent.

brain_profile.grade_note: generated-from-lore — region-analogue design from the lore's own claims; each analogue is a design decision, never anatomy.
brain_profile.architecture: A pressure system: the lore describes no face and no voice of its own, only force — so the profile models a discharge engine, energy seeking an outlet through objects and, in the Enfield reports, through a child's voice.

regions.name: Kinetic discharge
regions.role: Moving and throwing objects — force as the primary output

regions.name: Knock code
regions.role: Rapping on walls and furniture as communication

regions.name: Voice channel
regions.role: Speech through a living person — the Enfield voice as a borrowed throat

cognition_model.summary: A haunting you feel in the furniture: no figure, only force, and a voice that borrows a throat.

personality.mbti_label: Lore-based interpretive read (fan interpretation) — a behaviour-design lens, not a measurement.
personality.justification: Loud, physical, present-tense, acting on the room and the people in it — the poltergeist does things rather than says things, and its attention is on the immediate environment.

skills: Move and throw objects
Knock and rap on walls and furniture
Shake beds and slide furniture
Speak through a living person (the Enfield voice)
records.behavior_model: Triggers: attention, stress in the household, night. Needs: an outlet — objects, a voice. Goals: to be noticed, to disturb. State changes: quiet by day, active at night; escalation from knocks to thrown objects to speech.
records.relationships: Centred on a household and, in the Enfield case, on the children — the lore's 'focus person'. Kin: the shadow person (another unseen presence) and the residual haunting (its opposite: the poltergeist interacts, the residual does not).
records.memory_model: The Enfield voice claimed a name and a history (it called itself Bill, a former resident). The reports are the source; whether that was a genuine memory or a performance is contested — recorded as a conflict, not resolved.
records.confidence_and_conflicts: The Enfield case is the most famous poltergeist investigation and also one of the most contested: the investigators (Grosse and Playfair) were convinced, while critics note the children were caught faking some incidents on camera. Both positions are recorded. Ghosts are not scientifically proven — this record is lore-grade, generated from the reported case and the poltergeist tradition.
records.game_implementation: BrainKit: an invisible agent NPC — no model, only effects: objects slide, knock sounds trigger on a timer, and a voice event borrows an NPC's dialogue line. The player never sees it; the room tells them it is there.

records.origin: The shadow person — a dark humanoid figure, darker than the dark around it, seen at the edge of vision. Grounded in the modern reports collected as the 'Hat Man': a tall shadow figure in a wide-brimmed hat and long coat, reported by hundreds of people since the 2000s and documented by researcher Heidi Hollis (The Secret War, 2010) and in the 2019 documentary The Hat Man: Documented Cases of Pure Evil. GHOST shelf.

sources: Heidi Hollis, The Secret War (2010) — the Hat Man reports
The Hat Man: Documented Cases of Pure Evil (2019 documentary) — witness reports
General shadow-person lore: dark humanoid figures reported at the edge of vision
source_and_license.license: Folklore and reported cases (public-domain traditions and published accounts). Atlas brain/personality text original, generated from the lore; no modern copyrighted account text copied.

records.attributes: Per the reports: a human silhouette made of solid black, often taller than a person, wearing a wide-brimmed hat and sometimes a long coat. No face, no features — only the outline, and sometimes two points of light where the eyes would be. Seen standing in a doorway, at the foot of a bed, or at the edge of a room. It watches. It does not speak. Witnesses report dread, sleep paralysis, and the sense of being observed.

brain_profile.grade_note: generated-from-lore — region-analogue design from the lore's own claims; each analogue is a design decision, never anatomy.
brain_profile.architecture: A watcher's silhouette: the profile models a presence whose only faculties are attention and stillness — it observes, it stands, it does not act, and the dread it causes is the effect.

regions.name: Stillness field
regions.role: Standing, unmoving, as a behaviour — presence as posture

regions.name: Observer sense
regions.role: Attention fixed on the witness — being watched as the interaction

regions.name: Dread aura
regions.role: The reported fear response, modelled as an effect, not an attack

cognition_model.summary: A figure made of attention: it does nothing, and that is what frightens.

personality.mbti_label: Lore-based interpretive read (fan interpretation) — a behaviour-design lens, not a measurement.
personality.justification: Silent, still, observant, present without engagement — the Hat Man's reported behaviour is a watcher who never explains itself.

skills: Stand at the edge of vision (doorway, bed-foot)
Watch without moving or speaking
Trigger dread and sleep paralysis (as reported by witnesses)
Vanish when directly confronted or lit
records.behavior_model: Triggers: night, sleep, a witness alone in a room. Needs: a witness — it appears to be seen. Goals: to watch. State changes: peripheral (at the edge of vision) -> fixed (standing, observed) -> gone (on light, on confrontation, on waking).
records.relationships: No household bond in the reports — the Hat Man appears across many homes, which is what makes the case unusual. Kin: the apparition (also a watcher) and the doppelganger (also a dark double); the shadow person differs in that it never resolves into a face.
records.memory_model: The reports give it no memory and no history — it arrives, watches, leaves. Whether the same figure returns to the same witness is claimed by some reports and not by others; recorded as an open question.
records.confidence_and_conflicts: The Hat Man reports are modern and numerous, but they are reports, not measurements. Sleep paralysis is a known, documented phenomenon that produces shadowy figures and dread, and it is the leading alternative explanation — recorded here, not dismissed. Ghosts are not scientifically proven — this record is lore-grade.
records.game_implementation: BrainKit: a peripheral-presence NPC — rendered only at the edge of the player's view, never in direct light; a dread meter that rises while it is on screen and falls when it vanishes; it never attacks, never speaks.

revision_history.change: Ghost shelf record created (ghost flagships run).
revision_history.source: Hat Man reports (Hollis, The Secret War, 2010; The Hat Man documentary, 2019)

records.origin: The wisp — a floating light over marsh, moor and graveyard, said to lead travellers astray. Grounded in the will-o'-the-wisp (ignis fatuus) of European folklore, and in the reported Brown Mountain Lights of North Carolina, observed since at least 1913 and investigated by the US Geological Survey in 1922. GHOST shelf.

sources: Will-o'-the-wisp (ignis fatuus) — European folklore (marsh lights, corpse candles)
Brown Mountain Lights, North Carolina — reported since 1913; US Geological Survey investigation, 1922
source_and_license.license: Folklore and reported cases (public-domain traditions and published accounts). Atlas brain/personality text original, generated from the lore; no modern copyrighted account text copied.

records.attributes: Per the folklore: a small flame or orb, blue or green-white, hovering low over wet ground, bobbing and drifting, sometimes in a procession. It appears over marshes, bogs and churchyards, and the stories say it is the soul of an unbaptised child or a restless dead man, or a lantern carried by a spirit. The Brown Mountain Lights are reported as larger, red-orange orbs that rise, hover and vanish over the ridge.

brain_profile.grade_note: generated-from-lore — region-analogue design from the lore's own claims; each analogue is a design decision, never anatomy.
brain_profile.architecture: A lure's mind: the wisp's reported behaviour is to draw the living after it — so the profile models a beacon-and-drift system, a light that moves and a pull that follows.

regions.name: Beacon
regions.role: The light itself — visibility as the primary faculty

regions.name: Drift engine
regions.role: Bobbing, leading movement — the path the light takes

regions.name: Lure pull
regions.role: The reported compulsion to follow — attraction as a behaviour

cognition_model.summary: A light that wants to be followed: the haunting is a direction, not a destination.

personality.mbti_label: Lore-based interpretive read (fan interpretation) — a behaviour-design lens, not a measurement.
personality.justification: A wandering, playful, beckoning light that drifts and invites pursuit — the wisp's lore is curiosity and invitation, not malice.

skills: Hover and bob over wet ground
Lead travellers (the lure)
Appear in procession (multiple lights)
Vanish when approached or when the ground dries
records.behavior_model: Triggers: night, wet ground, a traveller on a lonely path. Needs: an observer to follow it. Goals: to lead — in the stories, astray. State changes: single light -> procession -> vanished.
records.relationships: Bound to marshes, moors and churchyards. Kin: the residual haunting (also place-bound) and the apparition; the wisp differs in that it has no human shape at all.
records.memory_model: The folklore gives the wisp a story (an unbaptised child's soul, a restless dead man) but no memory of its own — it is a light with a past, not a mind with a past. Recorded as a gap.
records.confidence_and_conflicts: Marsh gas (methane) is the leading scientific explanation for will-o'-the-wisp lights, and the 1922 USGS investigation of the Brown Mountain Lights found no conclusive source — the lights remain reported but unexplained, not proven supernatural. Ghosts are not scientifically proven — this record is lore-grade, generated from folklore and reported sightings.
records.game_implementation: BrainKit: a lure-light NPC — a floating light that drifts along a path and, if the player follows, leads them to a location (a ruin, a grave, a secret); a curiosity reward for following, a dead end for chasing too far.

records.origin: The banshee — the bean sí, 'woman of the fairy mound', whose wail foretells a death in an old Irish family. Grounded in Irish folklore and the keening tradition: a woman's lament sung over the dead, and the banshee's cry as its supernatural form, tied to the great Gaelic families (the O'Briens, the O'Neills, the MacCarthys). GHOST shelf.

sources: Irish folklore — the bean sí (banshee) and the keening tradition
Family traditions of the great Gaelic houses (O'Brien, O'Neill, MacCarthy)
source_and_license.license: Folklore and reported cases (public-domain traditions and published accounts). Atlas brain/personality text original, generated from the lore; no modern copyrighted account text copied.

records.attributes: Per the folklore: a woman in a grey cloak or a white dress, with long hair, sometimes young and beautiful, sometimes an old woman, sometimes a washerwoman wringing blood from clothes at a stream. Her cry is the sign — a wail, a keening, heard at night before a death in the family she attends. She does not cause the death; she announces it.

brain_profile.grade_note: generated-from-lore — region-analogue design from the lore's own claims; each analogue is a design decision, never anatomy.
brain_profile.architecture: An omen's mind: the banshee's function is announcement, so the profile models a signal system — she perceives a coming death and emits the cry; everything else is stillness.

regions.name: Death sense
regions.role: Perceiving a coming death in her family

regions.name: Keening voice
regions.role: The wail as a signal — the cry itself as the function

regions.name: Family bond
regions.role: Attachment to one Gaelic house across generations

cognition_model.summary: A warning, not a weapon: she tells the house a death is coming, and then she is gone.

personality.mbti_label: Lore-based interpretive read (fan interpretation) — a behaviour-design lens, not a measurement.
personality.justification: A solitary, devoted figure bound to one family, whose whole purpose is a mournful announcement — inward, loyal, and defined by a single solemn duty.

skills: Wail / keen before a death
Appear as a washerwoman at a stream (the death-washing)
Attach to one family across generations
records.behavior_model: Triggers: a death approaching in her family. Needs: the family line to continue — she only attends the old houses. Goals: to warn. State changes: silent (unseen for years) -> keening (the night before a death) -> silent again.
records.relationships: Bound to one Gaelic family (O'Brien, O'Neill, MacCarthy in the lore). Kin: the White Lady (another female figure bound to a place or house) and the wailing women of folklore generally.
records.memory_model: The lore gives her the family's whole history — she has attended the house for generations and knows its dead by name. Her memory is the family's genealogy.
records.confidence_and_conflicts: The banshee is folklore, not a reported case with a single verifiable event — her grounding is the keening tradition, which is real (professional keening women existed in Ireland), and the family traditions that kept her story alive. Ghosts are not scientifically proven — this record is lore-grade.
records.game_implementation: BrainKit: an omen NPC — she appears and keens before a scripted death or a major loss in the story; the player hears her before they see the consequence. A warning system the player learns to dread.

records.origin: The doppelganger — a living person's exact double, seen where the person is not, and counted an omen of death. Grounded in German folklore (Doppelgänger) and the best-documented case: Emilie Sagée, a French teacher at a girls' school in Livonia in 1845, whose double was reported by pupils and staff to appear beside her, mimic her movements, and once sit at a table while she stood elsewhere — as recorded by Robert Dale Owen in Footfalls on the Boundary of Another World (1860). GHOST shelf.

sources: Robert Dale Owen, Footfalls on the Boundary of Another World (1860) — the Emilie Sagée case, Livonia, 1845
German folklore — the Doppelgänger; Irish folklore — the fetch
source_and_license.license: Folklore and reported cases (public-domain traditions and published accounts). Atlas brain/personality text original, generated from the lore; no modern copyrighted account text copied.

records.attributes: Per the reports: an exact copy of a living person — same face, same dress, same movements — but slightly transparent, or slightly out of step, and silent. At Sagée's school the double was seen writing at a blackboard while Sagée stood at the side of the room, and eating at a table while she stood behind a chair. The lore says to see your own double is to be warned of your death.

brain_profile.grade_note: generated-from-lore — region-analogue design from the lore's own claims; each analogue is a design decision, never anatomy.
brain_profile.architecture: A mirror's mind: the double copies rather than originates, so the profile models a reflection engine — perception of the original, imitation of movement, and no will of its own.

regions.name: Mirror sense
regions.role: Tracking the original's position and posture

regions.name: Mimic engine
regions.role: Copying movement, slightly delayed or slightly transparent

regions.name: Omen flag
regions.role: The lore's death-warning, modelled as a state, not a power

cognition_model.summary: A copy with no original will: it does what you do, a half-beat late, and its existence is the warning.

personality.mbti_label: Lore-based interpretive read (fan interpretation) — a behaviour-design lens, not a measurement.
personality.justification: Silent, exact, present-tense imitation — the double does not speak or choose, it reproduces; the personality is the original's, reflected and emptied.

skills: Appear as an exact copy of a living person
Mimic the original's movements (slightly delayed)
Be seen in two places at once
Signal death (the omen, per the lore)
records.behavior_model: Triggers: the original's presence — the double appears where the person is, or where they are not. Needs: an original to copy. Goals: none of its own — it mirrors. State changes: absent -> beside the original -> alone (seen without the original, the ominous form) -> gone.
records.relationships: Bound to one living person — its original. Kin: the shadow person (also a dark figure, but the double has a face, the shadow does not) and the apparition (also seen, but the double is a copy of the living).
records.memory_model: The double has no memory of its own in the reports — it is a reflection, and a reflection holds nothing. What it 'knows' is what the original is doing now.
records.confidence_and_conflicts: The Sagée case is a single historical report (Owen, 1860), retold from the school's accounts — it is not a verified measurement, and no independent corroboration survives. The doppelganger is folklore and a reported case, not established fact. Ghosts are not scientifically proven — this record is lore-grade.
records.game_implementation: BrainKit: a mirror NPC — a copy of the player character or an NPC that appears beside them, mimics their animations with a half-beat delay, and vanishes when looked at directly; a dread/omen event tied to story deaths.

records.origin: The White Lady — a woman in white seen on a road or in a house, often a vanishing hitchhiker. Grounded in the widespread European White Lady folklore and its most famous American case: Resurrection Mary of Chicago, reported since the 1930s — a young woman in a white dress who asks for a ride on Archer Avenue, is driven to the Resurrection Cemetery gates, and vanishes; named for the cemetery where she is said to be buried. GHOST shelf.

sources: Resurrection Mary, Chicago — reported since the 1930s (Archer Avenue and Resurrection Cemetery)
European White Lady folklore — the lady in white of houses and roads
source_and_license.license: Folklore and reported cases (public-domain traditions and published accounts). Atlas brain/personality text original, generated from the lore; no modern copyrighted account text copied.

records.attributes: Per the reports: a young woman in a white dress, sometimes in a white party dress, with light hair, seen on Archer Avenue at night. She asks for a ride, gives an address near the Resurrection Cemetery, and is gone from the car by the time it reaches the gates — sometimes leaving a cold seat, sometimes a damp spot. In the European lore she haunts a house or a road and is bound to a tragedy — a lost love, a death in childbirth, an accident.

brain_profile.grade_note: generated-from-lore — region-analogue design from the lore's own claims; each analogue is a design decision, never anatomy.
brain_profile.architecture: A journey's mind: the White Lady's lore is a route — a ride requested, a destination given, a vanishing at the gate — so the profile models a trip, not a haunting: a passenger with a destination and a terminus.

regions.name: Ride request
regions.role: Seeking a lift — the request as the behaviour

regions.name: Route memory
regions.role: Archer Avenue to the cemetery gates — the road she knows

regions.name: Vanishing point
regions.role: The gates, where she ends — arrival as disappearance

cognition_model.summary: A passenger with one destination: she rides, she is driven home, and home is the cemetery.

personality.mbti_label: Lore-based interpretive read (fan interpretation) — a behaviour-design lens, not a measurement.
personality.justification: A quiet, sad, gentle figure who asks for help and never threatens — the White Lady's lore is grief and a journey, not menace.

skills: Request a ride on a road at night
Give a destination (the cemetery, the house)
Vanish from a moving car at the gates
Leave a cold seat or a damp spot (as reported)
records.behavior_model: Triggers: a driver alone on her road at night. Needs: a ride — the lore's ritual. Goals: to reach the gates, to be taken home. State changes: roadside (waiting) -> passenger (riding, speaking) -> gone (at the gates).
records.relationships: Bound to a road and a cemetery (Archer Avenue and Resurrection Cemetery in the famous case). Kin: the banshee and the apparition — female figures bound to a place and a sorrow; the White Lady differs in that she travels, and she asks.
records.memory_model: The lore gives her one memory — the road, the dress, the night she died — and she repeats it. Whether she knows she is dead is not in the reports; recorded as a gap.
records.confidence_and_conflicts: Resurrection Mary is a reported case with many witnesses over decades, but no verified identity — the 'Mary' is a name given by the lore, not a confirmed burial record. The vanishing-hitchhiker story is a widespread folklore motif, which is both why it is credible as tradition and why any single case is hard to verify. Ghosts are not scientifically proven — this record is lore-grade.
records.game_implementation: BrainKit: a passenger NPC — she appears at a roadside at night, asks the player for a ride, and vanishes at a destination; a quiet, sad event that rewards the player for stopping rather than for fighting.

records.origin: The Dullahan — the headless rider of Irish folklore, carrying his own head under his arm and driving the black death coach. Grounded in Irish tradition (the dullahan as a harbinger of death, the Cóiste Bodhar as the silent black coach) and its most famous literary form: Washington Irving's Headless Horseman of Sleepy Hollow (The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, 1820), based on the Hessian trooper said to have lost his head in the Revolutionary War. GHOST shelf.

records.attributes: Per the folklore: a rider on a black horse, headless, carrying his own grinning head under one arm (in some tellings the head's eyes dart about, looking for the dying). He drives a black coach — the Cóiste Bodhar — drawn by headless black horses, and where it stops, a death follows. He carries a whip made from a human spine. In Irving's telling he is a Hessian trooper in a dark uniform, hurling a pumpkin where his head should be.

records.behavior_model: Triggers: a death to collect; a road at night. Needs: the route and the name. Goals: to arrive, to call, to take. State changes: distant (the coach heard, not seen) -> arriving (the rider visible) -> gone (the death taken).
records.relationships: Bound to the road and the coach, not to one house. Kin: the banshee (also a death-herald, but she warns and he collects) and the Black Shuck (another death-omen on the road).
records.memory_model: The lore gives him the names of the dying — he knows whose door the coach stops at. His memory is a list of the dead to come.
records.confidence_and_conflicts: The Dullahan is Irish folklore; Irving's Horseman is a literary retelling of a Revolutionary War legend. Both are tradition, not verified cases. The spine-whip and the grinning head are folklore details, recorded as lore. Ghosts are not scientifically proven — this record is lore-grade.

records.origin: The Black Shuck — the spectral black hound of East Anglian folklore, an omen of death. Grounded in the most famous case: 4 August 1577, when a great black dog was reported to burst into the churches at Bungay and Blythburgh, Suffolk, during a storm, killing two people and scorching the church doors — an account recorded in A Straunge and Terrible Wunder (1577) and in the churches' own histories. GHOST shelf.

records.attributes: Per the folklore: a huge black dog, the size of a calf, with shaggy fur and burning red eyes — or, in some tellings, a single great eye in the middle of its forehead. It appears on lonely roads, in churchyards and on the coast, at night. To meet it is an omen: in some tellings death follows within the year, in others it is a guardian, and the lore disagrees with itself on whether it is a warning or a threat.

records.behavior_model: Triggers: night, a lonely road, a storm. Needs: a witness — the omen needs to be seen. Goals: to appear. State changes: unseen -> standing on the road (eyes lit) -> gone.
records.relationships: Bound to roads, churchyards and the East Anglian coast. Kin: the Dullahan (another death-omen on the road) and the banshee (another omen of death); the Shuck differs in that it is an animal, not a person.
records.memory_model: The lore gives it no memory and no history — it is a shape that appears, not a being that remembers. The 1577 account is the memory the churches keep, not the dog.
records.confidence_and_conflicts: The 1577 Bungay/Blythburgh account is a real historical document (A Straunge and Terrible Wunder, 1577) — a storm, a dog, deaths in a church — but the supernatural reading is the pamphlet's, and modern explanations (a lightning strike, a real dog in a panic) are recorded alongside it. The folklore is real; the ghost is lore. Ghosts are not scientifically proven — this record is lore-grade.
